articles.title: Report links Alaska Dems to secret effort to recruit would-be spoilers in Senate race
articles.summary: It was, for a while, considered one of those colorful quirks that crop up in the course of an election: the fact that not one but two candidates named Dan Sullivan will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot for U.S. senator from Alaska. One Dan Sullivan — Dan S. Sullivan — is the state's incumbent Republican senator. He is trying to fend off a fierce challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and secure a third term. The other Dan Sullivan — Dan J. Sullivan — is a retired teacher from a tiny fishing village along the Alaska Panhandle. He has never previously campaigned for public office, and he switched his registration from "unaffiliated" to "Republican " just before the deadline to run. (He has since switched back to unaffiliated .) But now the situation seems to be getting more serious. At President Trump's direction, the Justice Department last week sued in federal court to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant whose purpose is to siphon away votes. Then, on Wednesday, the New York Times published an extensive investigation that appears to substantiate that allegation , calling it "Democrats' secret effort to stack Alaska's ballot." "The Times has found, based on interviews and text messages, along with documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign, that not only did Ms. Peltola's team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader," the paper wrote. "The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent's support and help catapult the Democrat to victory." In response to the report, Trump called for both Peltola and the "fake" Dan Sullivan to be removed from the ballot in a post on Truth Social . Yahoo The outcome of the legal dispute, if it moves forward, could have enormous national implications. Democrats need to win at least a few Senate races in historically Republican states to secure a majority in the chamber. Polls suggest Alaska is one of their best chances to turn a red seat blue. Given how close other races across the country appear to be, a legal ruling that erases a narrow Peltola victory could be the pivot point that allows the GOP to keep control of the Senate for the last two years of Trump's presidency. How did this happen, and where do things go from here? Here's everything you need to know to catch up and make sense of the story. How Alaska wound up with two Dan Sullivans on the ballot Ballot-stacking — the process of recruiting a spoiler candidate to help your candidate win — isn't unheard of in politics, and the Times says it's "generally considered legal." But it's a lot easier in Alaska than other states because of the unique way elections work there. When Peltola ran for reelection to the U.S. House in 2024, the state GOP backed an effort to help a second Democrat — an inmate who conducted his campaign from a New York prison — remain on the ballot. And during this year's primaries, super PACs aligned with both parties "flooded the state with ads for fringe candidates" in an attempt to "dilute support for the mainstream candidates opposed by the groups," according to an October Alaska Beacon report . How is any of this possible? The Last Frontier sends the top four primary candidates to the general election regardless of party — then asks voters to rank them on Election Day in order of preference. This means that candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves. (Dan J. Sullivan initially claimed to be a Republican .) It also means that as ,long as they finish in the top four, primary candidates don't have to earn many votes to secure their very own ballot line on Nov. 3. (Dan J. Sullivan won 4,107 ). For months, Republicans have questioned Dan J. Sullivan's intentions and tried to get him tossed off the ballot. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court dismissed their arguments, ruling that neither state law nor the U.S. Constitution provided any legal basis for removing Dan J. Sullivan's name. How the Senate candidates will appear on Alaska's midterm ballot. elections.alaska.gov The more obscure Sullivan has "maintained that he [is] running in good faith and of his own volition, as a moderate Republican and not a secret Democrat," as a Times profile put it in August. He said he'd voted in the past for some Alaska Republicans, including Sen. Lisa Murkowski, even though he also "acknowledged previous donations to Ms. Peltola and a handful of other Democrats," and said he would prefer Peltola for Senate over the Republican incumbent "if it was between those two." But according to this week's Times report, "operatives aligned with" the Peltola campaign convinced Dan J. Sullivan to enter the race "to help Mary." The report cited as its sources 12 people "who participated in or were told of the plan" as well as interviews with other would-be recruits and dozens of internal text messages. For the record, both Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which directs the party's campaign strategy in Senate races across the country, have denied any "involvement," and Dan J. Sullivan did not respond to the Times's repeated requests for comment. One of the Times's main sources — former Peltola campaign manager and longtime aide Elisa Rios, who had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit — also tried to retract her statements to the paper ahead of publication. The Times story described an elaborate endeavor — which was "internally called the ballot composition project" — that "involved secret trips to far-flung Alaskan communities and the appearance of a mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs." The Times also reported that the "Peltola campaign's lawyers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee" were "involved" with the effort. The Trump administration's lawsuit Legal battles over the dual Dan Sullivan issue had been confined to state courts until last week. That's when Trump's administration filed its lawsuit aiming to have the certification of the results blocked if Peltola wins a close election that may have been affected by Dan J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot. "Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election," the Department of Justice wrote in its legal filing. "I'm the one that said do it," Trump said Friday of the lawsuit . The suit argues that a Democratic victory should be considered invalid if Peltola wins by a margin smaller than the total number of votes that Dan J. Sullivan receives — under the assumption that those votes may have come from confused voters who intended to vote for the incumbent Republican senator instead. Democrats have asked the courts to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the administration lacks "any statutory or constitutional authority to insert itself" into the state's electoral process. Alaska's state government, which is currently led by Republicans, has also filed to dismiss the administration's lawsuit. On Monday, a federal judge agreed to fast-track consideration of the dispute to potentially allow it to be resolved before Election Day. Many legal experts say the lawsuit has a slim chance of success. First, it requires a very specific outcome in which Peltola wins by what would likely need to be a very thin margin. Even in that scenario, election law experts say, the appearance of confusion on the part of voters does not create legal grounds for the federal DOJ to have the results rejected. "I believe that this lawsuit is abusive in its intentions and borders on frivolous in its arguments, and that it is destined for defeat in the courts should it reach the merits," Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, told the Alaska Beacon . Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a Harvard law professor, told the Harvard Gazette that the law the administration is relying on in its lawsuit — the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — does not give federal authorities any power to challenge state election procedures. "The lawsuit has nothing to do with voter registration. There's no allegation that anybody is improperly registered in Alaska; there's no claim that Alaska isn't in compliance with the NVRA's requirements for voter registration," Stephanopoulos said. More generally, experts say the lawsuit runs against the Constitution's language granting states the power to run their own elections. "This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," David Becker, a former Justice Department attorney who worked on voting rights cases, told Alaska Public Media . What's next? The federal judge in Alaska considering Democrats' motion to dismiss the lawsuit is expected to rule on whether Peltola's campaign and other groups can join the case on Wednesday. If that motion is granted, the judge said the DOJ should be ready to respond to a motion to dismiss the case by Thursday afternoon. That likely only matters in an extremely close race, which is not the recent norm in Alaska. The last time Dan S. Sullivan was on the ballot, he defeated his top challenger, independent candidate Al Gross, by 45,000 votes . The most recent Senate race, in 2022, was closer, but the top two finishers were both Republicans. Things are expected to be much tighter this time around. Peltola has held a consistent lead in the polls since the summer, but her advantage has steadily shrunk in the months leading up to Election Day. The most recent surveys have her ahead by 2 points, well within the margin for Sullivan to win. The Cook Political Report, one of the nation's most respected election forecasters, lists the race as a toss-up. Another well-regarded forecaster, the Center for Politics, categorizes it as "leans Democrat." articles.title: Hayden Panettiere's death ruled accidental by South Carolina police
articles.summary: The death of Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, South Caroline police announced Wednesday. Greenville Police Department said the investigation into Panettiere's death has been concluded "based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation," and the actor's death was officially ruled accidental. Last month, a South Carolina coroner confirmed Panettiere died from an accidental drug overdose that included fentanyl. There were no signs of trauma, the coroner's office said. Emergency responders were called to a residence where Panettiere, 36, had been staying in Greenville, South Carolina, on the afternoon of Aug. 16. Despite "advanced cardiac life support measures," she was pronounced dead there, the Greenville County Coroner's Office said.' Panettiere's on-again, off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach were at the scene of her death, according to a police report obtained by CBS News . The Hickersons made the 911 call that brought first responders to the apartment. Authorities, including the Drug Enforcement Administration, were investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death. Police previously said that a preliminary investigation "has not indicated any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances." articles.title: 2 right-wing provocateurs face election-related charges in Minnesota
articles.summary: Two right-wing provocateurs, James O'Keefe and Cam Higby, are facing election-related charges in Minnesota after posting videos of an undercover stunt intended to expose alleged deficiencies in election security . Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said each man faces a count of unlawful voting and identity theft. "Elections are the bedrock of democracy and their protection is one of our highest priorities," Moriarty said in a statement. "Individuals engaging in unlawful conduct related to our elections will be held accountable." Hegseth directs military cyber forces to use 'every authorized asset' to defend midterm elections from foreign interference amid Trump's funding cuts to election security agencies O'Keefe, a self-proclaimed "guerilla journalist" infamous for his undercover videos, and Higby, a social media influencer, posted the video at the heart of the charges in August. It shows the two men approaching election judges at multiple voting precincts in Minneapolis wearing burqas, speaking in fake accents, and allegedly misrepresenting their identities, in an effort to expose what O'Keefe and Higby say are gaps in the rules that allow residents to vouch for the identity of other voters. The video, which remains pinned on Higby's X account, is called "I Wore Burqa To EXPOSE Election FRAUD In Minneapolis." No ballots were cast in the course of their efforts. Tim Evans/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: People fill their ballots during the first day of early voting for the midterm elections in Minneapolis, Minnesota, October 16, 2026. Prosecutors said Wednesday that O'Keefe and Higby deceived the election judges by using the identities of real Minnesota voters "without those voters' knowledge or permission" in violation of state law. Each count carries up to five years in prison and a fine of up to $10,000. Neither man is in custody, according to charging documents. In a statement shared on X, Higby said, "No laws were broken. They want me in PRISON for exposing election vulnerabilities in their state." O'Keefe did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Steve Simon, the state's top election official, said in a statement that "any attempt to disrupt or deceive our election workers will not be tolerated." The charges announced Wednesday in Minnesota are not O'Keefe's first brush with the law. In 2010, O'Keefe pleaded guilty in Louisiana to a misdemeanor charge of entering a federal property under false pretenses after he posed as a telephone repairman to gain access to a U.S. senator's New Orleans office. articles.title: Trump praises Bolsonaro after he fled Brazil despite court order and criminal probe
articles.summary: As defeated right-wing Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro landed in Miami after fleeing his home country on Wednesday, Oct. 28, President Donald Trump said he approved of the move. "I think they’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible. It got bad reviews, and look what happened to their market," Trump told reporters outside Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday. Trump’s comments came only hours before Bolsonaro landed in Miami after the United States granted Bolsonaro and his family visas to enter the country. More: Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in Miami after fleeing Brazil Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, fled Brazil after a Brazilian judge ordered him to surrender his passport and barred him from leaving the country. The order came shortly after he lost the presidential runoff election. The court order also came as part of a criminal investigation into Bolsonaro’s alleged involvement in a money laundering scheme. Bolsonaro lost to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 81-year-old incumbent leftist, in the second round of the presidential election on Oct. 25 . The result surprised Bolsonaro, who led in the first round and was widely favored to defeat Lula da Silva, as he refused to concede and initially pledged to seek an annulment of the election, citing "foul play." Lula da Silva calls Bolsonaro fleeing Brazil 'shameful' Once news of Bolsonaro fleeing Brazil began circulating, Lula da Silva told supporters his opponent should have stayed in the country to prove his innocence, Reuters reported . "This act of leaving Brazil is shameful," Lula da Silva said. "When I was asked to surrender my passport, I did so. He should have done the same. If the Federal Police suspected he was going to leave Brazil, he ought to have surrendered his. Regrettably, that is the Bolsonaro family for you." Currently, Bolsonaro’s father, Jair, is serving a 27-year prison sentence after being found guilty of plotting against Lula da Silva in the aftermath of the 2022 election. Bolsonaro's younger brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who has resided in Texas since 2025, suggested during an Oct. 23 appearance on the "Louder with Crowder" podcast that his sibling should flee Brazil if he didn’t win the election. Flávio Bolsonaro said in a social media video that his brother’s comments prompted Brazilian authorities to order the surrender of his passport. Trump has criticized Brazil's voting process While Trump did not formally endorse Bolsonaro during the election, he has repeatedly criticized Brazil's voting process. "It looked like another rigged election, frankly," Trump said on Oct. 26. Trump has also condemned the criminal prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro, calling it a "witch hunt." The Trump administration imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil last year, a move, in part, motivated by the U.S. president's anger over Jair Bolsonaro's criminal trial. Contributing: Miles J. articles.title: 4 investigations Democrats could launch if they win control of Congress
articles.summary: Democrats have signalled a willingness to launch probes into both Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth's handling of the Iran war [Getty Images] Democrats in the US Congress are already planning how they would use their power if they win a majority in the House or Senate in next week's midterm elections. Success is by no means guaranteed, even if midterms can sometimes be brutal for the incumbent party that holds the White House. Control of the chamber, however, would give the party power to issue subpoenas - summons to testify or produce documents - as well as additional funding to launch investigations early next year. Democrats are weighing whether to investigate senior figures in the Trump administration - and possibly the president himself. Staffers have begun assembling a list of possible investigations and witnesses, according to people familiar with the discussions. Here are a few potential Democratic targets if the party emerges victorious on 3 November. 1. Trump's family and finances Democrats have made it clear that lucrative deals brokered by the Trump family's vast business empire will be primary targets of any initial investigations. "We want to make sure that [American] taxpayer dollars are being used wisely and not being stolen or pocketed because of corruption," Virginia Democratic Representative Suhas Subramanyam, a member of the House Oversight Committee, told the BBC. Items under consideration for investigation include ties between the administration and corporate entities -  particularly cryptocurrency firms -  as well as the international business dealings of the president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Other topics could include the $400m (£301m) aircraft gifted by Qatar to serve as Air Force One and multimillion-dollar defence contracts awarded to firms linked to the Trump family. "What's shocking to me is not only that this administration, cabinet officials and even the president and his family have been corrupt and self-dealing, but they've been so brazen and open about it," Subramanyam said. The White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing. "President Trump is focused on retaining Republican majorities in Congress and doubling down on the progress he has made to lower costs for families," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said. "Democrats have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to obstruct and baselessly target President Trump's commonsense agenda," she added. A White House official said the administration is "always prepared" to respond to oversight requests regardless of who is in Congress. [BBC] GUIDE: What are the US midterms? IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politicians EXPLORE: Where the US midterms will be won and lost VERIFY: How the US economy is really doing under Trump NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox 2. Hegseth and the Pentagon Democratic lawmakers have vowed to look into Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's handling of the war with Iran that began in February - including the number of civilian casualties, munitions shortfalls, spending and claims of poorly prepared troops and facilities. Other topics, according to a source familiar with the discussions, could include boat strikes in the Caribbean that the administration says are aimed at stopping the flow of drugs into the US. In April, a group of House Democrats filed rare articles of impeachment against Hegseth. They cited the war in Iran and accused him of "high crimes and misdemeanours". Impeachment requires only a simple majority in the House, but conviction - and removal from office - would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. No cabinet official has ever been removed this way. Some experts believe that the negative publicity that would come from congressional hearings could ultimately lead to Hegseth being fired or resigning from the position. "[If] it looks bad for the White House, and it's a drag on their media attention, President Trump might be likely to cut loose those officials, because he doesn't want that bad press," said David Miller, a political science professor and expert on the presidency at American University in Washington DC. "In a sense that could be a win for the Democrats." Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told the BBC that the decision to launch the war should come under scrutiny. "The bigger issue is this: this war was never authorised by the United States Congress, and I don't care who the secretary of defence is," he said. "The constitution says that Congress declares war," he said, and lawmakers should "haul these folks in" to answer questions. In a statement, Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson defended Hegseth's record, calling him a "transformative leader" who has "slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters". "By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under Secretary Hegseth's leadership than before," she said, using the administration's preferred name for the defence department. The aircraft gifted by Qatar to serve as Air Force One is also likely to be the target of Democratic investigations [Getty Images] 3. Immigration and ICE raids Senior Democrats -  including Robert Garcia, the California Democrat tapped to lead the House Oversight Committee should the party take back the chamber - have identified immigration enforcement as a key priority for potential congressional investigations. These could examine allegations of misconduct by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents during immigration raids across the country. But these investigations may prove difficult and politically tricky. In 2024, Trump campaigned on a promise of mass deportations of undocumented migrants - a message that resonated with many of his supporters. But recent polls suggest many Americans, including those who backed Trump in that election, are uncomfortable with some of the tactics used by ICE in American cities so far this year. It means Democrats will have to walk a fine line between opposing ICE tactics and appearing to dismiss broader immigration concerns, Painter told the BBC. 4. A third Trump impeachment Democrats are split on the possibility of attempting to impeach Trump for a third time. Some, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have expressed support for an impeachment, citing what they view as an unauthorised war with Iran and other alleged impeachable offences. Others have called for a more cautious approach, arguing that any impeachment is unlikely to end in the Senate voting to remove Trump - who has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing - from office. It is also unclear whether the party could agree on a reason to launch impeachment proceedings. "I can do whatever I want, if I want," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office in October, adding that he sees the impeachment efforts in his first term and the later criminal cases brought against him as "very illegal things". James Comer, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, told the Washington Sun news outlet in June that Democrats were "one-trick ponies" who were "going to go after Trump". There is no guarantee for Democrats that any potential investigation would end with a meaningful outcome. But Subramanyam said their efforts would send a message. "If we do not do something because we are scared of the optics, or we don't think it will be successful, or they stonewall us, that will be bad," he said. "Not just for the next two years, but for the next 20 years." articles.title: Trump floats Ted Cruz for Supreme Court and jokes about why he'd get every vote
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump floated nominating Ted Cruz to the Supreme Court for a future vacancy on the nation's high court, joking that the Texas Republican senator's confirmation would earn unanimous Senate support because senators from both parties would like to see him gone. Trump, who has mentioned Cruz previously for the Supreme Court, suggested the third-term senator again at an Oct. 27 midterm campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas as the president discussed what he might do if he gets to nominate a Supreme Court justice for a fourth time over his two White House terms. "I said, 'I have an answer to not being able to get it past the Democrats or the Republicans together,'" Trump said, referring to the confirmation fight in the Senate. "I would pick Ted Cruz to be the next Supreme Court justice, and I wouldn't have to worry about it. I wouldn't have to make a phone call. "The Democrats will 100% vote for it because they hate the guy and the want to get rid of him," Trump continued. "And the Republicans would 100% vote for it because they can't stand him, they would like to get rid of him. So I'd get 100% of the vote, and he would be a Supreme Court justice and he'd do a great job." More: Trump, Talarico hit different notes in dueling Texas rallies as Senate fight rages Cruz, who was in attendance at the rally for Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, laughed and smiled from his front-row seat as Trump made the pitch. A conservative firebrand in the Senate, Cruz has repeatedly said he's not interested in serving on the Supreme Court. ​“I don't want to be a judge,” Cruz told the Houston Chronicle in September. More: Trump says he regrets nominating Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, Barrett to SCOTUS Trump has openly expressed regret for nominating each of his three Supreme Court picks from his first term ‒ Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett ‒ after they sided against his administration in a series of high-profile rulings. Trump called Cruz "a brilliant guy, brilliant lawyer, brilliant all that." As solicitor general of Texas from 2008 to 2013, Cruz argued multiple cases before the Supreme Court. After graduating from Harvard Law School, Cruz clerked for then-Chief Justice William Rehnquist. Cruz, 55, has turned into one of Trump's strongest allies on the Senate after running against Trump for the Republican nomination for president in 2016. Cruz has also made no secret about his interest in running for president in 2028. Other Trump allies Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are also considered likely contenders to seek the Republican nomination. Were Trump to appoint Cruz to the Supreme Court, however, the field would start to narrow. It is unclear whether Trump will have an opportunity to nominate a fourth justice to the Supreme Court. Justice Samuel Alito in August said he plans to remain on the bench through at least the next session, batting down speculation the conservative justice could step down to allow Trump to choose his replacement. articles.title: Midwest Democrats face do-or-die moment to win back Trump districts before 2028
articles.summary: EAU CLAIRE, Wisconsin — In this rural-heavy stretch of the upper Midwest, Democrats are trying to claw back districts where their party brand is still deeply toxic. It won’t be easy, even in a midterm environment that heavily favors their party. Local Democratic organizers in western Wisconsin, where Rebecca Cooke is trying to oust GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden, know that elections here are decided by the slimmest of margins. They have no room for error. “Everything's on a razor's edge,” Clara Serrano, who volunteers for the local Democratic Party, said as she drove along farms and cornfields outside Eau Claire. But a decade after President Donald Trump’s populism and culture wars swung the formerly Democratic-leaning region right, many voters from western Wisconsin over to southern Minnesota and down to eastern Iowa are hurting — and blame the president’s policies. Family farms are reeling from his tariffs. Diesel is over $6 a gallon. The cost of fertilizer has shot up more than 30 percent since the war in Iran began earlier this year. “[Rural voters are] mad when we get to the door — and not at us,” said William Garcia, co-chair of the La Crosse County Democratic Party who has been out canvassing. “They're mad about gas prices. They're mad about fertilizer. They're mad about the tariffs. And so all we do as Democrats is say, ‘Hey, we agree. We rejected all of these things. We've been fighting all of these things.’ So it’s much more receptive now than really it's ever been.” Local Democrats have pulled out all the stops to propel Cooke in Wisconsin’s 3rd District, knocking endless doors in redder areas . There have been national reinforcements as well: Populist Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Cooke during the primary and hit the campaign trail with her this week in Eau Claire. The national party is trying to make generational gains in Minnesota’s 1st District — where they’re hoping to pull off a major upset to unseat GOP Rep. Brad Finstad in a Trump +12 district — and in deep-red Iowa, where Democrats are targeting three GOP House seats, a Senate seat and the governorship. Democrats for years have faltered with rural voters in these districts. Now, with polling showing Democrats gaining ground in redder territory and an electorate that’s souring on the GOP, Democrats hope they can finally make up ground this November — and lay a solid foundation for the 2028 presidential election. If that doesn’t happen, it’s an ominous sign for the party. “If we can’t win these seats now in this environment, it seems like we’re in for a world of hurt in 2028,” said one House Democrat, who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. Wisconsin Democrats have worked nearly-year round to build up a ground game. A major new initiative from the state party has helped to boost organizing, especially in rural counties and other places they’ve struggled. “We haven't really stopped organizing since 2024,” said Pete Huff, co-chair of the nearby Dunn County Democratic party, where Trump won by 16 points. Cooke, who grew up on a farm in the area, has tried to create a more durable brand of politics in the district by largely trying to distance herself from the national Democratic party as she seeks to win over a broader base of voters. It helped in 2024: She overperformed Kamala Harris by 9,000 votes across the district, even though she narrowly lost to Van Orden. “I think that the party doesn't know how to speak the language of rural America, and I feel like I uniquely do,” Cooke said in an interview. She regularly canvasses in rural communities and has tried to tie Van Orden to increasingly unpopular data center developments, after local projects sparked backlash. On Sunday, before the campus rally, Cooke attended a meeting for residents worried about a new high-voltage transmission line that would cut through farmland. This cycle, she’s especially leaned into the rare House endorsement from Sanders, who’s built his own populist and anti-establishment brand. At a Sunday rally on the University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire campus, she introduced the Vermont senator by saying: “Everyone forgets he’s an independent.” Potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders see the stakes of winning back rural-heavy districts as well. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is traveling to Minnesota’s 1st District on Sunday to rally voters for Democrat Jake Johnson in Rochester. It’s one of the many once-safe red seats that Republicans and Trump’s political operation are scrambling to shore up in these final days, with Johnson and Finstad running in what’s become a highly competitive race. Minnesota’s Democratic Gov. Tim Walz, then a high school teacher, won a House seat here in a 2006 wave election amid voter anger at the Iraq war and their GOP incumbent. Also that year, a local prosecutor named Amy Klobuchar swept to a big Senate win, part of a Democratic surge across the region. Democrats are hopeful that history is repeating, with high costs and a president unpopular because of a Middle East incursion hurting the GOP in the region and nationally. “The price of diesel is devastating,” said Ted Winter, who farms with his son near Fulda. “We've patterned a lot of our campaign after Amy Klobuchar, who famously shows up in every single county every single year,” Johnson, a math teacher, said in an interview. “And so I just said, ‘hey guys, let's host a town hall in every county.’” National Republicans for months brushed off concerns from local Republicans that Finstad’s race was growing increasingly competitive. Pro-Trump super PACs only recently injected their first cash of the race into the district, with the latest total quickly hitting several million dollars — an unheard-of prospect just a few weeks ago. The National Republican Congressional Committee spent for the first time in the race Tuesday. Democratic groups, on the other hand, started spending in the contest over the summer — and the leading House Democratic super PAC just responded with a $2.2 million money dump and a last-minute TV ad campaign . Finstad said in an interview at a local textile mill in Faribault that he flagged money concerns to national Republicans weeks ago. He also raised those concerns to GOP Whip Tom Emmer, who is from Minnesota. “We raised that with anybody and everybody that would want to hear it,” Finstad said. “From a global perspective, people were like, ‘Well, you won by 18, you're fine.’ And, you know, those of us in Minnesota know that this district has always had kind of an independent streak to it.” But Finstad said the tariffs were helping farmers in some cases, and the massive fraud scandals in Minnesota are keeping Trump voters and Republicans engaged in the final days. That’s one particular drag that could hit Johnson in this area. Democrats are still optimistic. “Things are changing in rural America right now,” Klobuchar, who’s now running for governor, told a crowd of volunteers and voters alongside Johnson on Sunday, at a local park in Fairmont. She pointed not only to the tightening 1st District race, but also to neighboring Iowa as proof. Republicans have grown particularly worried about the Hawkeye State as they’ve privately come to believe Democrats will flip at least one of three congressional seats there. And, they’re alarmed about the prospect of wider losses across a state Trump won by 13 percentage points, should disillusioned Republican voters decide not to turn out in the numbers they need.“Does it feel good to be running neck-and-neck against Democrats in Iowa just days out? No,” said one GOP strategist in Iowa working on a House race. But they noted that long-term demographic make-up of most Iowa districts do not favor Democrats. Speaker Mike Johnson is traveling to Rep. Zach Nunn’s Des Moines-based district in Iowa on Wednesday to help save the seat. Republican Joe Mitchell, who is running in the nearby seat to replace GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, is locked within the margin of error in his race against Democrat Lindsay James, according to two people with direct knowledge of internal polls. And Republicans are largely assuming GOP Rep. Mariannette Miller Meeks’ seat just to the south of that is already gone as she faces Democrat Christina Bohannan. “The tariffs, the Iran war, the health care cuts, these things are just brutal for the people of Southeast Iowa,” Bohannan said in an interview. That’s why national and local Democrats alike worry if they can’t pull out key wins in the upper Midwest this election season, they will continue to be shut out of power for years. They’re keenly aware that, no matter how frustrated rural voters are with Republicans, they’re still wary of the national Democratic party brand. “I don’t approach the door as a Democrat,” Jeremiah Fredrickson, who’s running to flip a Wisconsin state assembly seat, said in an interview before he knocked doors in the small, GOP-leaning village of Elk Mound. “My goal is to try to be a representative. I think way too many of our politicians have gotten to the point where they go to Madison, and they forget about the people back here.” At one door, an older man with white hair looked down at the pamphlet Serrano — the Democratic volunteer for Cooke and Fredrickson — was holding. “You can keep that,” he replied. “I’m not voting for them. No way in hell.” Van Orden, the Wisconsin Republican racing to hold his seat against Cooke, is skeptical his district’s voters will swing back toward Democrats. That’s despite high prices and Trump’s current unfavorability. The retired Navy SEAL rode in on his Harley-Davidson motorcycle to the Boon Docks bar as part of a multi-day district tour. After greeting patrons, he told POLITICO in an interview that Cooke is a “flat-out socialist.” He dismissed Sanders’ draw, saying that “voters here hate career politicians." “Is it politically convenient that we're fighting with the Iranians now? The answer is no,” Van Orden said. “I don't want gas prices to go up. I also don’t want my grandkids fighting the Iranians … 50 years from now.” But he’s counting on Trump voters to turn out for him. Across the bar, Deb Bork, who’s in her 70s and lives up the road in the small town of Independence, said she was sticking with Van Orden and Trump, regardless of the “hardship” of higher gas prices, saying the war was a blip compared to the length of other U.S. wars. She still trusts Trump. “He feels it's in the best interest of our country to protect us,” she added. “For so long we've been out there protecting everybody else and forgetting about the people that live here.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/28/democrats-rural-midwest-rebecca-cooke-01137050

articles.title: Tornado season isn't over, and fall twisters can bring added danger after dark
articles.summary: Shane Ostrander looks for items at his home after a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton swept through Fort Pierce, Florida, in October 2024. - (Kathleen Flynn/For the Washington Post) A second season of severe weather is about to ramp up across parts of the Plains, Mid-South and Gulf Coast. While tornado activity is most prominent in the springtime, autumn can bring a secondary peak.  These cool-season tornadoes skew faster, stronger and more likely to happen at night — and they can hit a more vulnerable part of the country. There are signs November may start busy, ahead of a winter that could bring above-average tornado risk due, in large part, to a strong El Niño pattern. Why do cool-season tornadoes happen? Tornadoes come from thunderstorms that form when air masses clash.  In the springtime, the coming summer warmth collides with the  retreat of winter. There’s plenty of heat and humidity to brew tall thunderclouds. Get Climate Coach newsletter News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free But in the autumn, cold air encroaches more forcefully.  Warmth is shunted south, and moisture is scant. Thunderstorms are more scarce, and when they do bubble up, they tend to be shallower — i.e., not as tall. Typically, a shorter thunderstorm would be weaker. In the wintertime, however, the atmosphere compensates. That’s because the jet stream —  the river of winds in the upper atmosphere — is strongest in the wintertime. And it dips southward over the Lower 48 states, tracing a serpentine pattern of crests and thoughts that propagate eastward. Even otherwise meager, low-topped thunderstorms tap into that jet stream energy above. Thunderstorms feel the robust wind shear, or changing winds with height, and can rotate. It’s not unheard of to have a cool-season storm cell too short to produce lightning — maybe only 15,000 or 20,000 feet tall — that still manages to rotate and produce a tornado. Where do they occur? In the fall, these storms happen where it’s warmest. That means the South. For much of the Deep South, November marks the unofficial start of a tornado season that will last until the start of summer. Tornado season is longer along the Gulf Coast than in any other part of the country. Mississippi averages 14 tornadoes between November and February — about 37 percent of its annual total. Alabama averages a dozen tornadoes, or 30 percent of its yearly average. Georgia and Louisiana get nearly a third of their tornadoes during the cool months, too. How do cool-season tornadoes differ? Cool-season tornadoes tend to have longer paths. That’s because they’re being yanked along  more quickly by the jet stream aloft. Most Read From The Washington Post The seven races that will decide control of the Senate Brazilian judge orders investigation into JD Vance donor network Grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson over Jan. 6 testimony What is the Cook Political Report, and why is Washington so obsessed with it? Why headlights seem more blinding than ever In Oklahoma, for example, wintertime tornadoes (the ones forming from November to February) have path lengths that are, on average, 46 percent longer than those during the rest of the year. In Mississippi, they’re 24 percent longer. And in Illinois, 58 percent longer. Longer paths expose more population to potential impacts , which is why the risk of deadly tornadoes is greater in the wintertime than during the heart of summer. Since recordkeeping began in 1950, November and December have had more killer tornadoes in the U.S. than July, August or September. Regional vulnerabilities Cool-season tornadoes also target areas of the Deep South and Southeast that can be more vulnerable — a region where mobile homes are common. Because there’s also less daylight, cool-season tornadoes are more likely to happen at night. That’s another factor that contributes to an increased death toll. There’s also emerging research that suggests cool-season tornadoes may skew a bit stronger, on average, than warm-season tornadoes. Although it’s unclear if that is because their faster forward speed combines with their rotational wind speeds. Alternatively, the actual tornado vortex may be stronger. Tornado season also lasts a long time in the South and Southeast. Consider Louisiana — its tornado season would run from Nov. 16 to May 21. That’s 187 days, or more than half the year.By our same definition, peak tornado season in Alabama would run from Dec. 16 to May 20, although activity often perks up sooner. Mississippi would be Dec. 7 to May 14. By comparison, in Oklahoma, peak tornado season lasts  two months — about April 10 to June 13. The Sooner State gets just as many tornadoes, but the season crams its twisters into a much shorter window. In North Dakota, peak tornado season is even shorter, just 57 days. In other words, the Great Plains have a springtime tornado frenzy. The Deep South and Southeast get a slow, painful season stretched over a longer window. How El Niño is playing a role This year’s cool-season tornado period may be enhanced by a strong El Niño pattern. El Niño begins as a warming of water temperatures in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. That heats the air above, causing it to rise. In turn, key global weather systems are shuffled around. Among them is the subtropical jet stream, which slices west to east across the Gulf of Mexico during El Niño winters. That has been known to increase cool-season tornado risk in the Deep South, especially Florida. Florida’s deadliest tornado outbreak happened during a strong El Niño winter. On the night of Feb. 22, 1998, into  the next day, intense tornadoes tore through the peninsula, including a pair of F3-strength twisters in the greater Orlando metro area. (The Fujita Tornado Intensity Scale rates wind-damage intensity on a scale of zero to 5.) Forty-two people were killed. articles.title: Trump scraps methane rules days after satellite spots plume near his Texas rally
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Tuesday pulled back regulations on a major global warming pollutant — just days after a satellite discovered a large plume of methane pouring out of oil and gas wells near the Lubbock, Texas, campaign rally where Trump made his announcement. Governments and the private sector are deploying a wave of new technology to pinpoint methane leaks like never before. But that technological revolution is colliding with political decisions in the U.S. and Europe to weaken regulations that are designed to curb the powerful driver of climate change. “The methane problem,” Trump said Tuesday night. “I'm officially terminating Biden's expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers $45 billion in costs, unlock vast quantities of Texas natural gas and produce 210 million barrels of oil.” American and European regulators alike have argued that the methane rules should be ditched or delayed because they threaten to increase the price and availability of energy, even as new technology identifies gas leaks — and bad actors — with remarkable accuracy. The backtracking could result in more methane emissions as nations around the world are failing to meet their commitments to contain climate change. “You can't reduce what you don't monitor,” said center-left European Parliament lawmaker Thomas Pellerin-Carlin, who opposes steps to delay the bloc’s rules. Methane has 80 times the warming impact of carbon dioxide over a 20-year period. Climate scientists say controlling methane, a byproduct of producing oil, gas and coal, along with agriculture and decomposing waste, is the fastest way to arrest rising temperatures. But the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has proposed weakening methane standards for oil and gas operators and is poised to eliminate penalties for so-called “super-emitters.” Meanwhile, the European Union is preparing to delay methane rules designed to prioritize energy imports with lower emissions. The backsliding comes as a wave of new technologies has pinpointed the world’s largest sources of methane, making it easier than ever before to prevent the gas from escaping into the atmosphere. A sweeping study published in the journal Nature found that methane-sensing equipment on satellites detected leaks with 92% to 100% accuracy on clear days, underscoring leaps in progress. Satellites are not the only improvement. Heat cameras can now spot leaks. Companies like Google are using artificial intelligence tools to map plumes from space. And firms are flying airplanes with a remote sensing technology that uses laser pulses, called LIDAR, to track methane. “Ten years ago, the tools were not there. You couldn’t detect these things,” said Riley Duren, CEO of the environmental nonprofit Carbon Mapper, which uses satellites and other technologies to detect methane leaks worldwide. “Today we have more tools at our disposal than ever. It’s not a visibility challenge anymore.” The group’s Tanager-1 satellite spotted methane leaks in a slice of the Texas Permian Basin on Oct. 10. Two days later, a new satellite named Tanager-2, which rode a SpaceX rocket into orbit this month, confirmed the Texas plume. The bigger test is getting companies to take action. Carbon Mapper this year has issued 460 notices to companies operating super-emitting sites in 13 U.S. states. It also works with California’s environmental regulator, the California Air Resources Board, on the only U.S. methane enforcement regime that uses satellite technology. Only about half of the recipients responded, Duren said. When asked why, he said states have differing levels of incentives — or punishments — to fix leaks. Many lack personnel. The absence of national policy doesn’t help. The story is similar across the world. The United Nations Environment Programme’s Methane Alert and Response System, which issues alerts from 35 satellites to 24 nations and nine subnational governments, registered a 12% response rate in 2025. The 141 governments that crafted methane reduction goals as part of the Paris climate agreement have done little to meet their targets: Just 20 countries have outlined steps to slash fossil fuel methane emissions, and only five have submitted quantified targets. “It’s clear that there’s a gap between what is being committed and what is being implemented,” said Marcelo Mena-Carrasco, CEO of the Global Methane Hub, a philanthropy-backed organization working to reduce emissions. “We know this in a much better way — we know who and which companies are doing so, and so we have all the elements to maintain accountability.” Except for enforcement regulations. Shifting geopolitics and a growing focus on securing energy supplies have pushed climate action down many countries’ priority lists. Industry has argued that many methane policies were ill-designed, and there has been pushback to what some companies viewed as a naming and shaming approach when emissions around their operations were identified, said Antoine Halff, who co-founded Kayrros, a firm that tracks methane emissions . The American Petroleum Institute, which represents U.S. oil and gas producers, praised Trump’s proposed rollback of the Biden-era methane limits. “We look forward to working with the Trump administration on a more workable approach that supports American energy production, provides greater regulatory certainty and advances continued emissions reductions,” Dustin Meyer, the group’s senior vice president of policy, economics and regulatory affairs, wrote in a statement. The current energy crisis resulting from the war in Iran has made governments anxious about taking any measures that could push up prices or curtail supply. Even though experts and the European Commission have said that the bloc’s incoming methane rules pose no risks to affordability or energy security, the fossil fuel industry, with the backing of the Trump administration , has seized on these worries to campaign for a delay — successfully. The Commission earlier this month proposed a one-year delay to rules meant to ensure oil and gas companies monitor and report their emissions. The requirement was supposed to inform a subsequent move toward curbing imports from the most polluting gas fields. The Commission also allowed countries to suspend penalties under the regulation. Then last week the European Parliament voted for a three-year postponement of the rules, and some EU governments are pushing for national capitals to adopt a similar delay, citing the energy crisis. Proponents of regulation have pointed out that by patching leaks, companies retain more gas to sell on the market. "We have independent scientific studies that show there is enough regulation-compliant gas on the market to supply the EU twice over. That means giving in to the lobbying right now is just a gift to the fossil fuel industry,” said German Green lawmaker Jutta Paulus. “After all, the gas that escapes unused is precisely what won’t end up on the market. In other words, we’re actually making the supply even scarcer rather than increasing it.” Smaller gas producers have long argued that measures to curb methane are costly. In the current environment, even bigger players who put in place measures to address their methane footprint are less interested in pushing forward. “The impetus toward certification of good methane and responsible gas and so on seems to be fading a bit,” said Halff. “I think this has to do with the extreme uncertainty in the market and concerns about energy security. … I think people are very comfortable pushing this discussion in the background to keep their options open in the future.” Methane measures haven’t completely halted. “There are definitely rollbacks in the U.S. In the EU, I would call it more of a delay than a rollback, but politically it is not the momentum that we would like to see. But I do think that in many other countries … we do have more positive success stories,” said Brandon Locke, director for global methane policy at the Clean Air Task Force, a nonprofit. China, the world’s largest methane producer, has included methane emissions in its latest national climate plan and created standards, rules and measuring and verification systems to curb coal mine methane, its biggest source of emissions . Japan and South Korea established a transparency initiative that asks liquefied natural gas suppliers to disclose their efforts to monitor and address methane leaks — though it’s based on self-reporting. And Kazakhstan, one of the world’s super-emitters due to its aging Soviet-era equipment, has dramatically reduced its methane emissions and is creating national rules to monitor them. That program is based on the EPA super-emitter program, which was enabled by advancements that allowed satellites to track performance across wider basins, said Duren, of Carbon Mapper. Canada’s enhanced methane regulations , which will take effect in 2028, prohibit flaring, put strict limits on venting and call for regular leak detection and repair. But they also allow oil and gas producers to determine how they’ll reduce their emissions, as long as they meet certain standards. The rules are weaker than those that were proposed during the Trudeau administration. “Where there has been sustained long-term efforts by governments to work with industry to systematically reduce emissions, there has been significant reductions and there's lower emissions,” said Stephane Germain, president of GHGSat Inc., which operates 20 satellites that continuously monitor and orbit the Earth. “I'll point to my own backyard here — British Columbia [and] Alberta — two jurisdictions where we rarely see anything with our satellites.” Those measures are all occurring at a time when energy demands are growing rapidly, and countries are using more coal and drilling for more oil to meet them. The U.N.’s latest assessment of the gap between what countries have committed to do on climate and what their policies will actually deliver shows that methane emissions haven’t fallen in the five years since countries pledged to drive them down 30% by 2030. That pledge, launched by the U.S. and EU, put methane on the map globally and mobilized billions of dollars in investment and a major new push on policy, including in China, said Rick Duke, a former deputy climate envoy at the State Department during the Biden administration. But the results of all that attention and money have been underwhelming, said Paulus, the German member of the European Parliament who negotiated the methane law. “We don’t need a Global Methane Pledge if no one's willing to do anything,” she said. articles.title: Hasan Piker sues CNN's Scott Jennings for defamation
articles.summary: Progressive Twitch streamer Hasan Piker filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative CNN commentator Scott Jennings on Tuesday, accusing him of falsely claiming Piker advocated for lynching Black Americans after airing an edited video of his remarks. The 38-page lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., centers on an Aug. 11 episode of “The Scott Jennings Show,” in which Jennings shared clips of Piker claiming he had said, “the USA should resume lynchings against Black people.” Piker, who threatened legal action in August over the claim and shared further context to the clips, alleges Jennings knowingly misrepresented sarcastic comments he made during his livestreams by turning it into an apparent endorsement of racial violence. “Mr. Jennings did not merely mischaracterize something Mr. Piker said,” the complaint reads. “He took a false, fabricated, and manipulated video of Mr. Piker, added a made-up quotation that Mr. Piker never uttered, and then made accusations that went beyond even what the manipulated footage purported to show.” During the August broadcast, Jennings warned Black voters to pay close attention before playing the clip, which included an on-screen caption attributing a statement, “Let’s go back to a better time when lynchings were happening,” to Piker. Jennings later accused Piker of “calling for Black voters to be lynched” and referred to what he called “the Piker plan of returning our country to lynchings.” The original footage came from an October 2024 Twitch broadcast in which Piker was reacting to a debate between two Black political commentators — one liberal and one conservative. After the conservative participant criticized “woke DAs,” Piker sarcastically suggested the commentator wanted to return to an era of racial discrimination and lynchings, according to the complaint. “He said, ‘We need more Klansmen, OK? Can we go back to a better time when lynchings were happening?’” Piker said during the stream in reaction to the commentator’s argument. Piker’s attorneys argue that the edited video removed the words “He said,” along with his laughter and surrounding commentary, to intentionally make it appear as though Piker was expressing his own beliefs rather than mocking someone else’s. The dispute emerged amid the Michigan Senate race , where the edited video was circulated to criticize progressive Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed over his association with Piker. When Jennings posted the segment on the social platform X, he referred to Piker as El-Sayed’s “best pal and campaign partner,” before accusing him of supporting racial violence. The post has received roughly 2.5 million views as of Tuesday, according to the lawsuit, and Jennings allegedly refused to retract his statements despite receiving a written demand from Piker’s attorneys on Aug. 31. Piker’s legal team also says the accusations damaged his reputation and threatened his ability to earn money through streaming, advertising and sponsorships. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. 5、 脑科学/脑机接口 | 据中证报报道，近日，由华中科技大学同济医学院附属同济医院牵头的脑机接口高质量数据集建设项目启动，旨在为脑机接口技术打造自主可控的“数据银行”。根据建设方案，该项目拟于2027年建成投用，聚焦脑卒中康复、脊髓损伤、帕金森病、癫痫、意识障碍、顽固性疼痛、面瘫、言语功能障碍、运动障碍性疾病和胃肠神经调控等10类疾病方向，基本覆盖神经调控与功能重建的主要临床场景。 点评：脑机接口作为连接人类中枢神经系统与外部数字世界的终极桥梁，当前正处于与AI深度融合的技术爆发期。支持政策密集落地，工信部等七部门《关于推动脑机接口产业创新发展的实施意见》、国家医保局为脑机接口单独立项、2026年“脑机接口”写入政府工作报告、“十五五”列为未来产业。机构预测，2030年全球脑机接口医疗市场400亿美元，2040年1450亿美元。 6、 算电协同 | articles.title: 美国原油库存四周连降，出口激增，馏分油库存降幅超预期
articles.summary: 原油供应持续收紧，叠加馏分油库存低于季节性均值，短期油价承压风险上升。 美国能源信息署（EIA）周三公布数据显示， 截至10月23日当周，美国商业原油库存连续第四周下滑，降幅超出市场预期，同期馏分油库存也进一步走低，但汽油库存意外大幅增加，折射出终端需求的分化走势。 此外 据华尔街见闻此前文章 ，伊朗无法接受卡塔尔本周日提交的停战草案，明确表示在核问题上不会让步。同时，美国已通过外交和军事渠道通知多个海湾阿拉伯国家，要求其在美国中期选举后为一场"短暂而激烈的军事行动"做好准备。 数据公布后，国际油价涨幅扩大——美国西德克萨斯中质原油（WTI）期货一度上涨3.6%，报每桶103.51美元。截至发稿，报每桶102美元。 分析人士指出， 馏分油库存持续低于季节性正常水平，柴油价格短期内难以获得有效缓解，而战略石油储备（SPR）释放节奏也明显放缓，市场缓冲空间日益收窄。 原油库存降幅超预期，出口大幅攀升 EIA数据显示，截至10月23日当周，不含战略石油储备的商业原油库存减少190万桶，至4.106亿桶，较五年同期均值低约4%。 据路透调查，市场此前预期库存增加1.5万桶；据《华尔街日报》调查，预期降幅为10万桶。 实际降幅显著超出两者预期。 从地区来看，俄克拉荷马州库欣交割枢纽库存减少62.4万桶，至2700万桶；墨西哥湾沿岸库存则降至2024年12月以来的最低水平。 与此同时，原油出口大幅上升，当周出口量增加140万桶/日至485万桶/日，净进口量则减少79.6万桶/日。 值得注意的是，船舶追踪机构Kpler对上述出口数据提出质疑。 该机构首席石油分析师Matt Smith表示，EIA公布的原油出口数据似乎存在明显高估，其追踪系统观察到的装载量约比EIA报告数据低100万桶/日，"这令库存平衡表中其他项目的准确性也存疑"。 馏分油库存持续偏低，柴油价格缺乏缓解空间 馏分油库存（含柴油和取暖油）当周减少150万桶，至1.028亿桶，较五年同期均值低约10%，降幅超出市场预期的90万桶。 同期馏分油需求则上升47.5万桶/日至420万桶/日。 TradeStation全球市场策略主管David Russell对此表示担忧： "能源库存降幅超出预期，出口带走了大量国内供应。馏分油库存持续低于季节性正常水平，意味着柴油价格短期内几乎没有下行空间。SPR释放节奏也已大幅放缓，这表明我们正在耗尽缓冲余地。" SPR当周仅小幅减少10万桶，至2.826亿桶，释放节奏的放缓进一步限制了政策工具对市场的支撑效果。 汽油库存意外大增，需求明显回落 汽油库存当周增加390万桶，至2.092亿桶，较五年同期均值低约2%。市场原本预期汽油库存将减少70万至90万桶，实际结果大幅偏离预期。 与此同时，汽油需求当周下降约62万至62.5万桶/日，至838万至840万桶/日。 Kpler的Matt Smith将这一现象描述为需求的"骤降"——汽油隐含需求明显萎缩，推动库存积累。不过他也指出，美国中西部地区汽油库存目前已处于历史低位，区域供需结构仍存在分化。 生产恢复，炼厂加工量小幅回落 此前因风暴导致停产的美国原油产量在本周出现恢复，当周日产量增加72.3万桶至1400万桶/日。原油进口量也有所回升，增加61.6万桶/日至640万桶/日。 炼厂端，当周原油加工量减少12.3万桶/日至1650万桶/日，炼厂开工率下降0.6个百分点至92.8%，略低于上周的93.4%。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 谷歌“网安高手”Gemini 4 Carbon登顶AI智能榜，漏洞检测得分88.2%，标准价持平Argon
articles.summary: 谷歌发布新一代旗舰模型Gemini 4 Carbon，在Artificial Analysis智能指数中以59分排名第一，漏洞检测得分达88.2%，安全代码生成成功率为前代Gemini 4 Argon的两倍多。Carbon首发API价格为每百万输入Token 2美元、输出Token 10美元，优惠结束后价格翻一倍，与Argon标准价格持平。 美东时间10月28日周三，谷歌正式发布Gemini 4 Carbon，称它为在网络安全防护和长周期处理能力方面最强的模型。这是谷歌在9月底推出Gemini 4系列旗舰模型Argon、并于10月中旬扩大其开放范围后，不到一个月内推出的又一款前沿模型。 谷歌表示，Carbon在编程、复杂推理、智能体工作流和网络安全防御方面均有进步，尤其针对需要长时间执行、多步骤规划和持续纠错的复杂工程任务进行了优化。 独立测评机构Artificial Analysis的最新评估显示，Carbon在其Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0中以59分位居榜首，超过Anthropic的Claude Opus 5.5和OpenAI的GPT-6 Astra。不过，Carbon并非在所有任务中都领先：在该机构的编程智能体指数中，它排名第二，仅次于Claude Opus 5.5。 与此前的Argon相比，Carbon进一步强化了谷歌在复杂任务执行和网络安全领域的竞争力。谷歌此次仍采取分阶段开放策略，首先通过Fairwind计划向经过筛选的网络安全防御者提供访问权限，随后再逐步向开发者、企业和消费者开放。 漏洞检测得分88.2%，安全代码生成成功率翻倍 网络安全是Carbon此次发布的核心卖点。谷歌表示，新模型在网络安全防御的多个环节均达到当前领先水平，覆盖漏洞发现、利用验证和漏洞修复，而不只是识别代码中的潜在问题。 在三项关键测试中，Carbon在SEC-bench Pro漏洞检测基准上的得分达到88.2%，在ExploitGym漏洞利用验证基准上得分为54.8%，在CWE-bench漏洞修复基准上得分为71.0%。 这些能力分别对应网络安全防御的不同阶段：首先发现真实软件中的漏洞，其次验证漏洞是否能够被实际利用，最后针对根本原因生成修复方案。对于企业和关键基础设施运营者而言，将这些环节衔接起来，有望减少人工排查和修补漏洞所需的时间。 谷歌还表示，在内部基准测试中，Carbon生成安全代码的成功率超过Gemini 4 Argon的两倍。谷歌Chrome团队报告称，在生成高质量补丁方面，Carbon的表现比另一家AI实验室的某款大型前沿模型高出10倍以上。 不过，上述网络安全成绩主要来自谷歌披露的测试结果，其中部分基准评估未启用安全防护措施，不能直接等同于模型在所有真实攻击和防御场景中的实际表现。对于具备漏洞发现和利用能力的前沿模型而言，如何确保能力主要用于防御而非恶意攻击，同样是商业化过程中必须解决的问题。 主动询问而非猜测，强化长流程任务执行与安全边界 除网络安全能力外，Carbon还针对复杂任务中的可靠性和执行边界进行了优化。 谷歌表示，新模型更擅长处理需要持续数小时甚至数天的复杂工程任务，包括在大型代码库和底层系统中定位隐蔽故障、分析问题根源并完成修复。模型能够在遇到阻碍后继续尝试，而不是轻易放弃。 在信息不完整或指令存在歧义时，Carbon也被设计为优先指出矛盾并向用户询问，而不是自行猜测后继续执行。谷歌希望借此减少智能体在复杂工作流中因误解要求而产生的错误。 在多步骤任务中，Carbon强调从规划到执行的完整性，同时遵守项目范围和权限边界。这对于能够自主修改代码、调用工具和执行连续操作的智能体尤为重要：模型不仅需要完成任务，还需要知道哪些操作未经授权、哪些信息仍需确认。 谷歌还称，Carbon在Gray Swan的间接提示注入基准测试中取得0.0%的攻击成功率，即抵御了该测试中所有被评估的攻击尝试。这是特定测试环境下的结果，并不意味着模型能够抵御现实世界中的所有提示注入攻击。 随着AI智能体开始承担更复杂的软件工程和企业自动化工作，模型的竞争标准正在从单纯的回答质量，延伸到执行可靠性、权限控制和安全边界。Carbon试图同时提升这些能力，以适应更高风险的企业级应用。 首发价格仅为标准价一半，优惠结束后与Argon持平 在定价方面，谷歌为Carbon提供限时首发优惠：每百万输入Token收费2美元，每百万输出Token收费10美元，缓存输入Token则享受95%的折扣。 按照这一优惠价格计算，缓存命中后的输入成本约为每百万Token 0.10美元。谷歌尚未确认此次首发优惠的结束日期。 Artificial Analysis披露，Carbon的标准价格为每百万输入Token 4美元、输出Token 20美元，缓存输入价格为每百万0.20美元。该机构在测评中采用标准价格，而非首发优惠价。换言之，Carbon的标准API价格与Gemini 4 Argon持平，首发优惠则将输入和输出价格均降低了50%。 Artificial Analysis的测算显示，按标准价格计算，Carbon完成一项该机构智能指数任务的成本约为7.76美元，比Claude Opus 5.5的10.04美元低约23%，但高于GPT-6 Astra的6.25美元。Carbon在该项评估中的平均输出量约为12.3万个Token，比Claude Opus 5.5少约29%。 这组数据表明，Carbon并非单纯依靠低价竞争，而是试图在复杂任务表现与执行成本之间取得平衡。对于需要长时间运行的编程智能体和企业自动化工作流，模型完成任务所需的Token数量、调用次数以及实际成功率，都会影响最终成本。 不过，Carbon目前尚未向所有开发者全面开放。其实际商业吸引力仍取决于后续开放节奏、任务完成质量以及优惠价格结束后的成本表现。 通过Fairwind计划先向防御者开放，参与美国政府预发布测试 尽管Carbon已经正式发布，谷歌并未立即向所有用户开放模型，而是继续采取分阶段部署策略。 谷歌表示，从本周开始，Carbon将首先提供给一部分网络安全防御者，随后通过Fairwind计划逐步扩大至更多可信合作伙伴。谷歌将根据早期用户反馈持续调整安全防护措施，再逐步向开发者、企业和普通消费者开放。 Fairwind是谷歌面向政府机构、企业客户及网络安全合作伙伴推出的有限访问计划，目标是利用前沿AI协助发现、验证和修复软件漏洞，保护关键基础设施、公共服务和企业系统。 谷歌同时表示，公司正在参与美国政府的自愿预发布模型测试流程。这意味着Carbon不仅需要接受常规的模型能力评估，还将纳入发布前的安全测试与风险评估安排。 这一部署方式与谷歌此前推出Gemini 4 Argon时采取的策略一致：先向经过筛选的网络安全防御者开放，让专业机构有机会使用模型强化防御，再逐步扩大访问范围。随着前沿模型在漏洞发现、代码生成和自主执行方面的能力增强，如何在扩大商业应用的同时降低潜在滥用风险，已成为谷歌发布新模型时必须权衡的问题。 总体来看，Gemini 4 Carbon在独立智能指数中登顶，并在漏洞检测、安全代码生成和复杂任务执行方面取得进展，显示谷歌正加快追赶前沿AI竞争对手。其下一阶段的关键，将是能否在保持安全防护的前提下扩大用户覆盖，并将基准测试中的优势转化为企业实际工作流中的可靠表现。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 报道：AI融资弄潮儿Pimco见好就收，砍半Meta和甲骨文债券仓位，躲过大跌
articles.summary: 全球最大固定收益资产管理机构之一太平洋投资管理公司（Pimco）在人工智能基础设施债券热潮中大举押注，随后通过一系列时机精准的减持操作， 在市场价格大幅回落前锁定盈利，成功规避了困扰同类投资者的巨额账面亏损。 据彭博援引知情人士透露， Pimco在参与AI债券市场的同时，已大幅削减旗下最大仓位，部分持仓建立仅数月便完成出售。 该公司对今年以来数桩大型AI融资交易选择回避，包括博通与Anthropic联合发行的大额债券，以及软银集团约110亿美元的垃圾债。 上述动作表明，这家债券巨头对AI债券市场的态度已明显趋于审慎。 目前，支撑甲骨文密歇根数据中心园区的相关债券已从发行价98.7美分跌至约88美分。博通等其他大型AI债券近期同样承压，报价约为96美分。 多重价格下行信号之下，AI债券市场的风险正引发业界广泛关注，部分投资者已将此轮热潮与互联网泡沫时代相提并论。 锚定投资者优势，两笔旗舰交易均实现盈利出局 Pimco最具代表性的AI债券投资，是2024年参与了Meta平台公司路易斯安那州大型数据中心项目的融资——该笔交易规模约180亿美元，被市场称为"Beignet"，并成为此后众多AI数据中心融资的参照模板。 Pimco于买入后六至八个月内抛售了约30亿美元，彼时该债券交易价格高于面值，初期一度涨至110美分以上。 随后，Pimco又在甲骨文密歇根数据中心园区融资中投入约100亿美元。 据知情人士透露，Pimco作为上述两笔交易的锚定投资者，以明显低于官方发行价的折扣价认购，从一开始便为自身设置了安全垫。 监管文件显示，Pimco目前两笔仓位均已减持约50%，减持时点均在债券价格较高位时完成。 根据行业价格报告系统Trace的数据，甲骨文密歇根州债券目前已回落至约88美分，较发行价大幅下滑。Pimco尽管仍是这两笔交易的最大持有人之一，但大规模套现已使其整体风险敞口显著收窄。 主动回避多宗大型交易，对AI债市转趋保守 在成功锁定前期收益的同时，Pimco今年明显加大了对新增AI债券投资的筛选力度。 知情人士透露， 该公司选择不参与博通与Anthropic联合发行的大额债务交易，同时亦回避了软银集团规模约110亿美元的垃圾债发行，以及与甲骨文相关的新墨西哥州数据中心贷款项目。 这一态度转变与Pimco在私募信贷市场的一贯立场相吻合。作为私募信贷繁荣的知名批评者，Pimco长期警示该行业贷款标准趋于松弛——目前私募信贷市场规模已膨胀至逾1.8万亿美元。 不过，Pimco并未全面退出AI领域。据彭博报道，该公司近期购入SpaceX一笔大型融资交易中价值40亿美元的份额，以支持SpaceX拓展其人工智能相关业务。此举显示Pimco仍在选择性布局，而非系统性撤退。 AI债券市场压力显现，行业争议升温 价格下行的压力已在整个AI债券市场蔓延。甲骨文密歇根州项目债券和Meta路易斯安那州项目债券近期均出现下跌，博通相关债券报价亦跌至约96美分。 Meta首席执行官扎克伯格上周向投资者表示，公司将更大力度押注AI，导致Meta股价走低，其债务违约保险成本创下历史新高。 围绕AI债券热潮是否存在泡沫风险，业内观点分歧明显。据彭博报道，城堡投资（Citadel）创始人Ken Griffin上周表示，企业仍在应对AI带来的深远影响，包括在该技术上的投入规模及其对经济的潜在冲击。 黑石集团总裁Jon Gray则持较为乐观的立场。他在黑石公布季度业绩后接受采访时表示："说到泡沫，人们通常想到的是先建产能、再等待需求到来。而AI恰恰相反——你在建产能的同时，担心的是能否跟上需求。" AI企业已公开披露其庞大的数据中心与芯片开发支出计划，这种规模性烧钱态势，正促使越来越多的投资者重新审视这场热潮的可持续性。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 沃什押注“生产率提升” 一场掩耳盗铃的豪赌！？
articles.summary: 美联储周三（10月28日）宣布，将联邦基金利率目标区间维持在3.75%至4%不变。 因为不加息符合预期，所以市场几乎没动。 但如果你把这份声明从头到尾读一遍，你会发现一件奇怪的事：声明在描述一个热得发烫的经济体：增长强劲，国内支出有韧性，投资旺盛，就业跟得上劳动力增长，失业率没怎么变，同时通胀仍然偏高，照这个思路走下去，怎么看结论都是加息。 9月FOMC全票加了25个基点，当时对经济形势的判断还只是“稳健”，这次升格成“强劲”，同时通胀还没下来，有什么理由停？ 沃什在两点半的记者会上对此进行了解释：生产率提高了，经济就有空间跑得更快、跑得更久，同时不推高物价。 这是一个漂亮的说法，但本质上是在赌博。

articles.summary: 1、【美联储按兵不动】美联储周三（10月28日）宣布，将联邦基金利率目标区间维持在3.75%至4%不变。此前其在9月加息25个基点。12名票委中有2人投票反对，主张再加息25个基点，其中包括特朗普一直试图罢免的理事丽莎·库克。 2、【加拿大央行三年多来首次加息至2.5%】加拿大央行10月28日宣布将政策利率上调25个基点至2.5%，为2023年7月以来首次加息。此前，央行已连续七次议息将利率维持在2.25%不变。央行表示，此举旨在降低持续高企的能源价格广泛传导至其他商品和服务价格的风险。 3、【美司法部问询英伟达收购Hugging Face】10月28日，据路透社援引两位知情人士报道，美国司法部已就英伟达以129.3亿美元收购开源平台Hugging Face一事展开问询，评估交易对人工智能领域竞争的影响；与此同时，执法部门针对这家芯片巨头商业行为的多年期调查仍在推进。知情人士称，官员们追问的核心是：这笔交易会否让英伟达握住AI的一个基础性分发节点。问询还涉及英伟达可能如何借助该平台损害AI市场上的竞争对手、获取筹码；官员们同时在了解Hugging Face竞争对手的情况。 4、【欧洲气价自2022年以来首破100欧元】欧洲天然气价格28日（周三）升破每兆瓦时100欧元（约合111美元），为2022年以来首次，美国的价格仅约8.5欧元。自美国和以色列首次对伊朗动武以来，欧洲气价已涨至原来的三倍以上。战事造成供应中断，而冬季临近之际库存又处于低位。欧洲如今面临“又一场能源危机”。 5、【伊朗拒绝卡塔尔停战方案】伊朗一名高级官员28日对路透社表示，卡塔尔斡旋人员带来的方案“不可接受”，伊方不会在核问题上表现任何灵活性。几乎同时，《华尔街日报》援引知情人士披露，美国已告知多个海湾阿拉伯国家，为11月3日中期选举后一场“短促而猛烈”的对伊军事行动做好准备。
